title: The house the villagers built — yang, taken further
goal: Build the relative clauses English builds with “which”, “that” and “whose”: *yang* followed by a passive verb, and *yang* followed by a noun with *-nya*. And stop saying *di mana* where Indonesian does not want it.
bekal: describe things by what was done to them: *rumah yang dibangun warga*, *kopi yang saya beli*
say “whose” the Indonesian way: *ibu yang anaknya kuliah di UGM*
replace the English-flavoured *di mana* and *yang mana* with *tempat*, *ketika* or plain *yang*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Keliling desa
dialogs.intro: The first days of April 2028. Before the first homestay guests arrive, Pak Harun walks Sarah along the guided route he wants to offer. Sarah plays the tourist and asks everything a tourist would.

lines.text: Makanya rute ini saya usulkan. Tamu yang datang dari kota suka cerita.

lines.text: Setelah ini kita lewat sawah yang kebanjiran bulan lalu itu?

lines.text: Ya, lalu mampir di warung yang pemiliknya menjual kopi Menoreh.
lines.id: Yes, and then we stop at the stall whose owner sells Menoreh coffee.
lines.literal: yes, then drop-in at stall that owner-its sells coffee Menoreh.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Sempurna. Semua yang Bapak sebutkan tadi sudah saya catat.
lines.id: Perfect. I've written down everything you just mentioned.

notes: **Joglo** is the classic Javanese house with a tall, stepped roof held up by four central pillars (*saka guru*). Old joglo are prized, expensive and sometimes bought whole and moved to Bali, which says something about how rare an intact village one is.

**Rumah yang dibangun warga** — “the house the villagers built”. English simply drops “that” and keeps the active verb; Indonesian turns the verb passive and puts the doer straight after it, with no *oleh*. This single pattern is the heart of the unit, and the grammar box explains why it is compulsory.

**Gotong royong** is working together unpaid for the common good: repairing a road, building a hall, cleaning the drains before the rains. It is also a political word, repeated in speeches since the 1940s, so you will meet it in villages and in newspapers alike.

**Bu Sumi, yang suaminya penabuh kendang** — the comma matters. Without it (*Bu Sumi yang suaminya…*) you are picking out which Bu Sumi; with it you are just adding information about the one everyone knows. Written Indonesian marks this with a comma exactly as English does with “who”.
**Kebanjiran** is the *ke-…-an* of misfortune from A2 Unit 11: something *happened to* the fields. *Sawah yang kebanjiran* is “the fields that got flooded”; *banjir* on its own is just “flood”.

**Semua yang Bapak sebutkan** — “everything you mentioned”. Inside a *yang* clause the pronoun passive works too: *yang saya beli*, *yang kamu bilang*, *yang Bapak sebutkan*. Addressing Pak Harun as *Bapak* rather than *Anda* is the polite “you” — Unit 13 will say more.

grammars.title: yang + passive: “the thing that someone did something to”
body: Indonesian *yang* can only point at the **subject** of the clause that follows it. So when the noun you are describing is the thing that was built, bought or read, the verb must turn passive to make that noun its subject.

head: Indonesian
Word for word
English
rows: coffee that is-sold at stall that
the coffee sold at that stall
the problem we have to solve

after: ⚠️ *Rumah yang warga membangun* is wrong, and so is *buku yang saya membaca*. If the doer is a pronoun (*saya, kamu, kita, Bapak*), use the bare verb after it; if it is a noun (*warga, turis*), use *di-* and put the noun after the verb.

When the described noun **does** the action, nothing changes: *warga yang membangun rumah itu* — “the villagers who built that house”. Ask yourself one question every time: is my noun the doer or the done-to?

grammars.title: yang + noun-nya: how Indonesian says “whose”
body: There is no word for “whose”. Instead, *yang* is followed by the possessed thing with *-nya* pointing back: “the woman who her-son studies at UGM”.

head: Indonesian
Word for word
English
rows: woman who child-her study at UGM
the woman whose son studies at UGM
the tree whose leaves are turning yellow
the stall with the friendly owner
the house with the leaking roof
a village whose people stick together

after: English often says “with” where Indonesian uses this pattern: “the house with the leaking roof” is still *rumah yang atapnya bocor*. Once you notice it, you will hear it constantly.
The last row combines both halves of this unit: possessor *-nya* plus a pronoun passive. Read it slowly and it falls into place.

dialogs.title: Second dialogue — Draf brosur Yoga
dialogs.intro: The same afternoon, at the project desk in the village hall. Yoga, the UGM intern, has written the first brochure for Sumberwangi and wants Sarah to check it.

lines.text: Mbak, draf brosurnya udah jadi. Coba dicek, deh.
lines.id: Sarah, the brochure draft's done. Have a look.
lines.literal: Miss, draft brochure-the already finished. try be-checked, [deh].

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Oke. “Sumberwangi adalah desa di mana Anda bisa menikmati sunrise.” Hmm.
lines.id: OK. “Sumberwangi is a village where you can enjoy the sunrise.” Hmm.
lines.literal: OK. Sumberwangi is village at where you can enjoy sunrise. hmm.

lines.speaker: Yoga:

lines.id: What? It sounds cool, doesn't it?

lines.text: Kedengarannya seperti terjemahan. Lebih baik: “desa tempat Anda bisa menikmati matahari terbit.”
lines.id: It sounds like a translation. Better: “a village where you can watch the sun rise.”
lines.literal: sounds like translation. more good: village place you can enjoy sun rise.

lines.text: Oh, jadi “di mana” cuma buat pertanyaan?
lines.id: Oh, so “di mana” is only for questions?
lines.literal: oh, so at where only for question?

lines.text: Kurang lebih begitu. Bu Lestari pasti mencoret yang ini.
lines.id: More or less. Dr. Lestari would definitely cross that out.
lines.literal: less more like-that. Mrs Lestari surely crosses-out which this.

lines.speaker: Yoga:
lines.text: Terus, “homestay yang mana dikelola ibu-ibu desa” gimana?
lines.id: And what about “homestays which are run by the village women”?
lines.literal: then, homestay which is-managed mothers village how?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: “Mana”-nya dibuang saja: “homestay yang dikelola ibu-ibu desa”.
lines.id: Just drop the “mana”: “homestays run by the village women”.
lines.literal: which-the is-thrown just: homestay that is-managed mothers village.

lines.speaker: Yoga:
lines.text: Wah, Mbak Sarah lebih galak daripada dosen pembimbing saya.
lines.id: Wow, you're stricter than my thesis supervisor.
lines.literal: wow, Miss Sarah more fierce than lecturer supervisor my.

lines.text: Bukan galak, Yog. Brosur yang rapi bikin tamu percaya.
lines.id: Not strict, Yoga. A tidy brochure makes guests trust you.
lines.literal: not fierce, Yog. brochure that neat makes guest trust.

lines.speaker: Yoga:
lines.text: Siap, Bu Editor. Saya revisi sekarang juga.
lines.id: Yes, Madam Editor. I'll revise it right now.

notes: **Coba dicek, deh** — Yoga's request is passive: “try it being checked”. Indonesians very often ask for things this way (*coba dilihat*, *silakan diisi*), and it sounds softer than *cek, deh*. *Deh* adds a friendly push, like “go on”.
**Desa tempat Anda bisa…** — *tempat* (“place”) is the everyday replacement for relative “where”. No *yang* is needed after it, and no *di*: *rumah tempat saya lahir*, “the house where I was born”.

**The irony is deliberate.** Many young, educated Indonesians write *di mana* and *yang mana* because they read so much English, and a foreigner who has learned the rules may notice it first. Editors, teachers and the language centre (*Badan Bahasa*) all flag it.
**Mencoret** is to strike out with a pen; *coretan* is a scribble or a crossed-out bit. Supervisors' *coretan* on a thesis draft are a rite of passage at every Indonesian university.

**Galak** — fierce, strict, bad-tempered; used of dogs, teachers and landladies. *Dosen pembimbing* (often just *dospem*) is a student's thesis supervisor, the most feared and most discussed person in a final-year student's life.

**Siap!** — literally “ready!”, from military and police speech — is now a cheerful “on it!” among young people and in offices. *Yog* is Yoga's name clipped to one syllable, a very common affectionate habit: *Sar*, *Rin*, *Yog*.

grammars.title: ⚠️ di mana and yang mana: the English calques
body: *Di mana* and *yang mana* are questions (“where?”, “which one?”). Used as relative pronouns they are borrowed from English “where” and “which”, and careful Indonesian replaces them.

head: Calque (avoid)
Natural Indonesian
English
rows: the house where I was born
a time when everyone is asleep
the year when the big flood happened
a situation where we have to choose

after: *Di mana* is perfectly correct as a question (*Di mana toilet?*), inside an indirect question (*Saya tidak tahu di mana dia tinggal*) and in *di mana-mana*, “everywhere”.
You will hear the calque in speeches and on television, so do not be surprised by it. But in anything written that matters, use *tempat*, *ketika* or a plain *yang*.

sections.title: yang clauses on signs and in brochures

blocks.text: Official notices love *yang* clauses because they let you address a group without naming anyone. Read these as you would see them on the walls of a homestay or a tourist site.

head: Notice
English
rows: *Tamu yang menginap wajib melapor ke pengelola.*
Overnight guests must report to the management.
*Barang yang tertinggal bukan tanggung jawab kami.*
We are not responsible for items left behind.
*Pengunjung yang membawa anak harap mengawasi anaknya.*
Visitors with children are asked to supervise them.
*Sampah yang dibawa harap dibawa pulang kembali.*
Please take home any rubbish you bring.
*Kamar yang sudah dipesan tidak dapat dibatalkan.*
*Kendaraan yang diparkir di sini akan diderek.*
Vehicles parked here will be towed.
*Paket yang ditawarkan sudah termasuk makan pagi.*
The packages on offer include breakfast.

blocks.text: Notice that three of these use *yang* + passive (*dibawa, dipesan, diparkir*) because the thing described is the thing acted upon — exactly the rule from Dialogue 1.

sections.title: tempat, ketika, cara: the nouns that do the work

blocks.text: English relative words like “where”, “when”, “how” and “why” have no single Indonesian twin. A plain noun usually takes their place, with or without *yang*.

blocks.title: Three quick tests before you write di mana
items: Is it a question? Then *di mana* is fine.
Is it a place? Try *tempat*.
Is it anything else? Try plain *yang*, or rewrite the sentence.

blocks.text: 💬 In fast speech *tempat* and even *yang* sometimes disappear (*warung kami biasa makan*), but keep them in writing. And *di mana* inside a sentence is still correct when it hides a real question: *Saya lupa di mana saya parkir motor* — “I forget where I parked the motorbike”.
Cover the Indonesian column, read the English, and rebuild each sentence from memory.

*Permisi, Pak Darto. Kami dari tim desa wisata. Boleh minta waktu sebentar untuk survei?*

Right, this is my kebaya from when I was a girl. Go on, try it on.

Isn't that too much trouble? The ceremony is on Sunday, remember.
